sources.title: Catawba Nation: About the Nation
sources.note: Direct tribal account, We Are Proud of Our Past and Our People. Conflicting Hagler dates and termination typo in Our Heritage are not adopted; historical population and purity superlatives excluded.

sources.title: National Park Service: Southeast Chronicles, Ninety Six
sources.note: Direct Brief History of the Catawba section: coalescence, Yamasee War and Revolutionary displacement. Does not imply all regional Siouan peoples became Catawba.

sources.title: R. P. Stephen Davis Jr.: Archaeology of the Catawba Nation after the Treaty of Pine Tree Hill
sources.note: Direct one-page 2017 Office of State Archaeology lecture abstract. 1760 treaty and 15-mile-square reservation; Old Town, Ayers Town and New Town.

sources.title: Mary Elizabeth Fitts: Variability in Maize from Eighteenth-Century Catawba Towns
sources.note: Direct primary poster PDF, Methods, Introduction and Conclusions; 171 cob sections from 13 pits. Cultivar inference explicitly tentative, no unsupported assignment of every pit to hide smoking.

sources.title: Catawba Nation: Catawba Pottery
sources.note: Direct Our Cultural Legacy, manufacture, inherited tools, open firing and women selling pots. Avoids unqualified oldest/purest and precise four-thousand-year continuity claims.

sources.title: Catawba Nation Archives: Records of the Catawba Indian Nation Government
sources.note: Direct CING Administrative history: 1840 land claim, 1959 termination, 1973 petition and 1993 recognition.

sources.title: Catawba Nation: Suuk Hinu Child Care
sources.note: Direct first body paragraph explicitly pairs Suuk Hinu with Seed House; contemporary childcare curriculum.

sources.title: Catawba Nation: Walking Trails
sources.note: Indexed original Cultural Center Trail description: replica village structures and present-day garden. Direct open cache miss; indexed text checked, not a physical archaeological garden dated to antiquity.

sources.title: Library of North Carolina: Tuscarora People
sources.note: Indexed original complete article, revised 2025, Thomas Parramore and colleagues. Upper/Lower Town distinction and Indian Woods; obsolete evaluative language excluded.

sources.title: North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources: Nooherooka marker
sources.note: Indexed original complete marker essay; archaeology of bunkers, tunnels, food and 1.5-acre fort. Casualty totals not treated as modern exact census.

sources.title: East Carolina University: Tuscarora focus of ECU archaeology site
sources.note: Direct 7 June 1995 university excavation report, site and 1713 destruction. Does not adopt Phelps’s obsolete last-native-culture assertion, mistaken Georgia attribution or disputed exact final day.

sources.title: National Park Service: The Six Nations Confederacy During the American Revolution
sources.note: Direct Tuscarora admission around 1720 and Revolutionary War paragraphs; no exact prehistoric confederacy date or unqualified uniform national alliances adopted.

sources.title: United States Supreme Court: Federal Power Commission v. Tuscarora Indian Nation, 362 U.S. 99
sources.note: Direct 1960 majority and dissent in historical judgment, reservoir condemnation of fee-owned lands. Not presented as current legal advice or a decision extinguishing nationhood.

sources.title: National Museum of the American Indian: Gauntlet/Cuff
sources.note: Indexed full collection record NMAI_209797; wool, hide and glass beads, raised beadwork; purchased by Heye in 1937. Production date unknown, place inferred.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Anthropological Archives: J. N. B. Hewitt photographs
sources.note: Indexed original finding aid printed p.11, Box 1 Folder 8 Items II.35-42; named Tuscarora beadwork sellers at Niagara Falls. Collection range circa1897-circa1937; no invented date for individual photos.

sources.title: Institute for Tribal Environmental Professionals: Tuscarora climate profile
sources.note: Direct primary interview profile, document dated August 2011 (not 2024 upload); p.2 heirloom seed program, intercropping, canning and pressure-cooker photo caption.

sources.title: Sam Bosco and Brad Thomas: Skaru:rę Food Forest, Planting and Seedling Pickup
sources.note: Direct first-person project account, event 25 May 2019, Cornell researcher and Tuscarora collaborator. About30 plants at school, workshops and cooking; no botanical misidentifications copied.

sources.title: Paris Harper: The Tuscarora Migration in 1713 and 2013
sources.note: 2013 University of Georgia MA field research, printed p.5 Note on Terminology. Direct fetch403; exact indexed original query site:openscholar.uga.edu/record/11058 "Skaru" "People of the Shirt" yields paragraph and original spelling Skaru:rȩɂ with both translations.

sources.title: Tuscarora Nation: Official community contacts and programs
sources.note: Direct official site, Lewiston NY office, health center, school and Nęyękwawętaʔθkwáhshek language program. Linked language website unavailable, so no sample inferred from its program name.

sources.title: East Carolina University: Nooherooka 300
sources.note: Direct 15 March 2013 announcement, Tuscarora delegates, map conservation and planned migration commemoration. Planned attendance/journey not reported as completed.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Single Catawba record only. Decoded first polygon in world_1492 spans Carolina Piedmont, bbox [-82.5506,34.05395,-80.4698,36.21891]. 1492 to 1715 preserved as imported coverage. Subsequent coalescence, settlements and living Nation explicitly distinguished; no automatic absorption of other Siouan identities.

Do not repair silently: first decoded polygon in world_1492 bbox [-76.41616,42.37369,-75.60256,42.83129] is central New York. It is anachronistic for 1492 to1500 North Carolina homeland and does not depict modern Niagara reservation. Public overview states both. Narrative follows Carolina Upper/Lower Towns, Indian Woods, early18c migration/confederacy and living NY Nation; no claim that every Carolina Tuscarora migrated.
